claims.claim: No evidence of a ring of inward-directed forces was produced by the TgMyoA knockout parasites.
claims.source: In stark contrast to the wild-type parasites, we also saw no evidence by traction force mapping of a ring of inward-directed forces produced by the TgMyoA knockout parasites.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from traction force mapping of TgMyoA knockout parasites.

claims.claim: No displacement of the matrix above background noise was detected by TgMyoA knockout parasites.
claims.source: In fact, we did not detect any displacement of the matrix above background noise by these parasites (compare Figure 6B to Figure 6D and E; see also Figure 6—figure supplement 1, n=16 parasites), suggesting that any forces produced by the moving knockout parasites are below the limit of detection in our traction force assay.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B, 6D, 6E, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1 from analysis of 16 parasites.

claims.claim: Any forces produced by the moving TgMyoA knockout parasites are below the limit of detection in the traction force assay.
claims.source: In fact, we did not detect any displacement of the matrix above background noise by these parasites (compare Figure 6B to Figure 6D and E; see also Figure 6—figure supplement 1, n=16 parasites), suggesting that any forces produced by the moving knockout parasites are below the limit of detection in our traction force assay.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that no displacement above background was detected.

claims.claim: The motility defect in parasites lacking TgMIC2 is less severe than the defect in parasites lacking TgMyoA.
claims.source: The motility defect in parasites lacking TgMIC2 (Gras et al., 2017) is less severe than the defect in parasites lacking TgMyoA, with 36 of 297 TgMIC2 knockout parasites (12%) capable of moving more than one body length (see also Gras et al., 2017; Huynh and Carruthers, 2006).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from analysis of 297 TgMIC2 knockout parasites and citations to prior work (Gras et al., 2017; Huynh and Carruthers, 2006).

claims.claim: 36 of 297 TgMIC2 knockout parasites (12%) are capable of moving more than one body length.
claims.source: The motility defect in parasites lacking TgMIC2 (Gras et al., 2017) is less severe than the defect in parasites lacking TgMyoA, with 36 of 297 TgMIC2 knockout parasites (12%) capable of moving more than one body length (see also Gras et al., 2017; Huynh and Carruthers, 2006).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from analysis of 297 TgMIC2 knockout parasites.

claims.claim: TgMIC2 knockout parasites often move in an erratic, stop and start pattern, bending sharply and moving in tightly twisting arcs.
claims.source: However, these parasites often moved in an erratic, stop and start pattern, bending sharply and moving in tightly twisting arcs (Figure 6A and Video 12).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A and Video 12.

claims.claim: TgMIC2 knockout parasites fail to form constrictions.
claims.source: The TgMIC2 knockout parasites also failed to form constrictions and did not detectably deform the fibrin matrix (Figure 6C, n=36 parasites, Figure 6—figure supplement 2, n=18 parasites) despite being able to move at maximum speeds similar to wild-type parasites (Gras et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 2 from analysis of 36 and 18 parasites respectively.

claims.claim: TgMIC2 knockout parasites do not detectably deform the fibrin matrix.
claims.source: The TgMIC2 knockout parasites also failed to form constrictions and did not detectably deform the fibrin matrix (Figure 6C, n=36 parasites, Figure 6—figure supplement 2, n=18 parasites) despite being able to move at maximum speeds similar to wild-type parasites (Gras et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 2 from analysis of 36 and 18 parasites respectively.

claims.claim: TgMIC2 knockout parasites can move at maximum speeds similar to wild-type parasites.
claims.source: The TgMIC2 knockout parasites also failed to form constrictions and did not detectably deform the fibrin matrix (Figure 6C, n=36 parasites, Figure 6—figure supplement 2, n=18 parasites) despite being able to move at maximum speeds similar to wild-type parasites (Gras et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature (Gras et al., 2017).

claims.claim: Motility is significantly altered, but not completely eliminated, in parasites lacking TgMyoA or TgMIC2.
claims.source: Taken together, these data confirm that motility is significantly altered, but not completely eliminated, in parasites lacking TgMyoA or TgMIC2.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing reduced but not absent motility in knockout parasites.

claims.claim: Both TgMyoA and TgMIC2 are required to produce the constrictions and the constriction-associated inward forces on the matrix observed during the motility of wild-type parasites.
claims.source: Furthermore, the data demonstrate that both proteins are required to produce the constrictions and the constriction-associated inward forces on the matrix observed during the motility of wild-type parasites.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data showing that knockout of either protein eliminates constrictions and detectable forces.

claims.claim: The nuclei of parasites lacking TgMIC2 do not change shape as they move in 3D.
claims.source: The nuclei of parasites lacking TgMIC2 did not change shape as they moved in 3D (Figure 7A and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A), providing further evidence that these parasites do not undergo the constrictions seen in wild-type parasites.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: Parasites with and without TgMIC2 travel along trajectories of similar mean length (38±9 µm vs. 42±8 µm, respectively).
claims.source: While parasites with and without TgMIC2 traveled along trajectories of similar mean length (38±9 µm vs. 42±8 µm, respectively), parasites lacking TgMIC2 moved approximately half as far from their starting point as wild-type parasites (Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: Parasites lacking TgMIC2 move approximately half as far from their starting point as wild-type parasites.
claims.source: While parasites with and without TgMIC2 traveled along trajectories of similar mean length (38±9 µm vs. 42±8 µm, respectively), parasites lacking TgMIC2 moved approximately half as far from their starting point as wild-type parasites (Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: The circumferential zone of attachment to the matrix functions to convert meandering motility into more linear, directed forward progression.
claims.source: These data suggest that the circumferential zone of attachment to the matrix, which requires TgMIC2, functions to convert meandering motility into more linear, directed forward progression.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that TgMIC2 knockout parasites have less directional movement.

claims.claim: The predominant forces exerted by a moving parasite are periodic and directed in toward the parasite at a fixed circular location within the extracellular matrix.
claims.source: We show here using three-dimensional traction force mapping that the predominant forces exerted by a moving parasite are instead periodic and directed in toward the parasite at a fixed circular location within the extracellular matrix.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from 3D traction force mapping experiments.

claims.claim: The highly localized forces are generated by the parasite pulling on the matrix.
claims.source: These highly localized forces, which are generated by the parasite pulling on the matrix, create a visible constriction in the parasite's plasma membrane.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the direction of the force vectors and the observation of constrictions.

claims.claim: The ring of inward-directed force corresponds to a circumferential attachment zone between the parasite and the matrix, through which the parasite propels itself to move forward.
claims.source: We propose that the ring of inward-directed force corresponds to a circumferential attachment zone between the parasite and the matrix, through which the parasite propels itself to move forward.
claims.evidence: This is a proposed interpretation of the experimental data.

claims.claim: In parasites lacking TgMIC2, neither the inward-directed forces nor the constriction of the parasite membrane are observed.
claims.source: In parasites lacking the major surface adhesin, TgMIC2, neither the inward-directed forces nor the constriction of the parasite membrane are observed.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from TgMIC2 knockout parasites.

claims.claim: The trajectories of TgMIC2-deficient parasites are less straight than those of wild-type parasites.
claims.source: The trajectories of the TgMIC2-deficient parasites are less straight than those of wild-type parasites, suggesting that the annular zone of TgMIC2-mediated attachment to the extracellular matrix normally constrains the directional options available to the parasite as it migrates through its surrounding environment.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing trajectories of wild-type and TgMIC2 knockout parasites.

claims.claim: The annular zone of TgMIC2-mediated attachment to the extracellular matrix normally constrains the directional options available to the parasite as it migrates through its surrounding environment.
claims.source: The trajectories of the TgMIC2-deficient parasites are less straight than those of wild-type parasites, suggesting that the annular zone of TgMIC2-mediated attachment to the extracellular matrix normally constrains the directional options available to the parasite as it migrates through its surrounding environment.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation that TgMIC2 knockout parasites have less directional movement.

claims.claim: Parasites of the phylum Apicomplexa are responsible for approximately one million deaths annually.
claims.source: Parasites of the phylum Apicomplexa cause pervasive human disease and are responsible for approximately one million deaths annually (World Health Organization, 2021; Sow et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (World Health Organization, 2021; Sow et al., 2016).

claims.claim: Toxoplasma gondii is the most prevalent apicomplexan parasite.
claims.source: Toxoplasma gondii is the most prevalent apicomplexan parasite, infecting 30–40% of the human population worldwide (Bigna et al., 2020; Flegr et al., 2014; Pappas et al., 2009).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Bigna et al., 2020; Flegr et al., 2014; Pappas et al., 2009).

claims.claim: During invasion of host cells by T. gondii, proteins secreted from the parasite's apical organelles assemble a ring-shaped zone of tight attachment between the membranes of the two cells.
claims.source: During the invasion of host cells by T. gondii and other apicomplexan parasites, proteins secreted from the parasite's apical organelles assemble a ring-shaped zone of tight attachment between the membranes of the two cells.
claims.evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge about apicomplexan invasion.

claims.claim: The moving junction is anchored to the host cytoskeleton and provides a fixed platform against which the parasite exerts force.
claims.source: This 'moving junction' does not in fact move: it is anchored to the host cytoskeleton and is hypothesized to provide a fixed platform against which the parasite exerts force (Alexander et al., 2005; Besteiro et al., 2011; Dubremetz, 1998; Lebrun et al., 2005; Porchet-Hennere and Torpier, 1983; Aikawa et al., 1978).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Alexander et al., 2005; Besteiro et al., 2011; Dubremetz, 1998; Lebrun et al., 2005; Porchet-Hennere and Torpier, 1983; Aikawa et al., 1978).

claims.claim: The body of the parasite narrows dramatically as it passes through the moving junction during invasion.
claims.source: The body of the parasite narrows dramatically as it passes through the moving junction, bearing a striking resemblance to the constrictions we report here during 3D motility.
claims.evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge about parasite invasion.

claims.claim: TgAMA1 and TgRON2 are central players in moving junction formation in T. gondii.
claims.source: Two central players in moving junction formation in T. gondii are TgAMA1, an adhesin secreted onto the parasite surface from the micronemes, and TgRON2, which is secreted by the parasites into the host cell plasma membrane and serves the ligand to which TgAMA1 binds.
claims.evidence: This is a statement based on established knowledge about moving junction formation.

claims.claim: Neither TgAMA1 nor TgRON2 plays any detectable role in parasite motility.
claims.source: Neither TgAMA1 (Bargieri et al., 2013; Mital et al., 2005) nor TgRON2 (RVS and GEW, unpublished data) plays any detectable role in parasite motility.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Bargieri et al., 2013; Mital et al., 2005) and unpublished data.

claims.claim: TgMIC2 likely plays an analogous role during motility to that of TgAMA1 during invasion, with TgMIC2 binding to ligands in the extracellular matrix rather than to TgRON2 in the host cell membrane.
claims.source: Instead, TgMIC2 – another microneme protein secreted onto the parasite surface – likely plays an analogous role during motility to that of TgAMA1 during invasion, with TgMIC2 binding to ligands in the extracellular matrix rather than to TgRON2 in the host cell membrane.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the experimental data and comparison with invasion mechanisms.

claims.claim: As the parasite moves forward during both invasion and 3D motility, it simultaneously rotates around its long axis.
claims.source: As the parasite moves forward during both invasion and 3D motility, it simultaneously rotates around its long axis (Leung et al., 2014; Håkansson et al., 1999; Pavlou et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Leung et al., 2014; Håkansson et al., 1999; Pavlou et al., 2018).

claims.claim: The TgMyoA motor driving invasion and motility is arranged helically within the parasite, along the spiraling subcortical microtubules.
claims.source: It has long been proposed that the TgMyoA motor driving invasion and motility is arranged helically within the parasite, along the spiraling subcortical microtubules (e.g. Pavlou et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature (Pavlou et al., 2020).

claims.claim: The unique geometry of the parasite periphery can generate a self-organized helical pattern of anterior-to-posterior actin flow.
claims.source: Alternatively, a recent modeling study suggests that the unique geometry of the parasite periphery can generate a self-organized helical pattern of anterior-to-posterior actin flow (Hueschen et al., 2022).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature (Hueschen et al., 2022).

claims.claim: If actin filaments flow helically and are connected to the tails of transmembrane adhesins engaged circumferentially with the host cell surface or extracellular matrix, the forward motion of the parasite will be accompanied by rotational twist.
claims.source: In either case, if the actin filaments flow helically and are connected to the tails of transmembrane adhesins engaged circumferentially with the host cell surface or extracellular matrix, the forward motion of the parasite either into the cell or through the matrix will by definition be accompanied by rotational twist.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from the proposed mechanism of helical actin flow and circumferential attachment.

claims.claim: Some portion of the perpendicular force directed towards the annular constriction may reflect torque on the matrix produced by the parasite as it twists through this circular zone of attachment.
claims.source: Some portion of the perpendicular force that we observed directed towards the annular constriction in our traction force assays may in fact reflect torque on the matrix produced by the parasite as it twists through this circular zone of attachment.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the experimental data.

claims.claim: As a parasite invades a host cell, antibodies are 'shaved' off the parasite surface at the moving junction by an as yet unknown mechanism.
claims.source: As a parasite invades a host cell, antibodies are 'shaved' off the parasite surface at the moving junction by an as yet unknown mechanism (Dubremetz et al., 1985).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature (Dubremetz et al., 1985).

claims.claim: A similar phenomenon of antibody shedding is observed during 3D motility.
claims.source: Remarkably, a similar phenomenon is observed during 3D motility: fluorescent antibody against the surface protein TgSAG1 is lost from the parasite surface anterior to the constriction and shed as a helical trail of fluorescence behind the moving parasite (Figure 5—figure supplement 2 and Video 10).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2 and Video 10.

claims.claim: 3D motility can be described as the parasite undergoing sequential invasion-like events through circular zones of attachment to the matrix.
claims.source: For example, our data suggest that 3D motility can be best described as the parasite undergoing sequential invasion-like events through circular zones of attachment to the matrix; during invasion the parasite only needs to move a single body length to penetrate into the host cell, but during motility the parasite can string multiple constriction events together to move multiple body lengths (Figure 5C).
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data suggesting a mechanistic similarity between motility and invasion.

claims.claim: The characteristic constriction of the parasite seen at the moving junction during invasion may reflect the parasite attaching to and pulling on the host cell plasma membrane as it penetrates, rather than being squeezed as it pushes through.
claims.source: The data also raise the possibility that the characteristic constriction of the parasite seen at the moving junction during invasion does not reflect the parasite being squeezed as it pushes itself through the small diameter opening into the host cell, as is commonly thought (e.g. Herm-Götz et al., 2002; Mordue et al., 1999), but rather the parasite attaching to and pulling on the host cell plasma membrane as it penetrates.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the data with citations to prior work (Herm-Götz et al., 2002; Mordue et al., 1999).

claims.claim: Actin polymerization is nucleated at the apical tip of the parasite by formin1.
claims.source: The data presented here with wild-type parasites are at least partially consistent with the linear motor model of motility, in which: (a) actin polymerization is nucleated at the apical tip of the parasite by formin1 (Tosetti et al., 2019); (b) TgMyoA translocates the actin filaments in an anterior-to- posterior direction along the length of the parasite; and (c) binding of the rearward flowing actin filaments to transmembrane adhesins (Jacot et al., 2016), whose extracellular domains are attached to the substrate, drives the forward motion of the parasite (Figure 1A).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature (Tosetti et al., 2019).

claims.claim: Anterior-to-posterior actin flux may occur along the entire length of the parasite periphery.
claims.source: While anterior-to-posterior actin flux may occur along the entire length of the parasite periphery (Hueschen et al., 2022; Quadt et al., 2016; Stadler et al., 2017), we propose a modification to the linear motor model in which force is generated, in whole or in part, by the rearward translocation of the subset of actin filaments that are coupled to adhesins at the circular ring of attachment.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Hueschen et al., 2022; Quadt et al., 2016; Stadler et al., 2017).

claims.claim: Force is generated by the rearward translocation of the subset of actin filaments that are coupled to adhesins at the circular ring of attachment.
claims.source: While anterior-to-posterior actin flux may occur along the entire length of the parasite periphery (Hueschen et al., 2022; Quadt et al., 2016; Stadler et al., 2017), we propose a modification to the linear motor model in which force is generated, in whole or in part, by the rearward translocation of the subset of actin filaments that are coupled to adhesins at the circular ring of attachment.
claims.evidence: This is a proposed modification to the linear motor model based on the experimental data.

claims.claim: No anterior-to-posterior bias in the force vectors at the constriction was detected.
claims.source: We were unable to detect any anterior-to-posterior bias in the force vectors at the constriction, which would be expected if the parasite pulls against this zone of attachment in order to move forward.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from traction force mapping.

claims.claim: The regularity with which the parasite generates circular zones of attachment could be due to periodic bursts of formin1-mediated actin polymerization at the parasite's apical tip.
claims.source: The regularity with which the parasite generates the circular zones of attachment on its surface, yielding on average one constriction per body length of motion (Figure 5C), could be due to periodic bursts of formin1-mediated actin polymerization at the parasite's apical tip (Tosetti et al., 2019) or to periodic release of adhesins such as TgMIC2 from the micronemes.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the data with citation to prior work (Tosetti et al., 2019).

claims.claim: The regularity with which the parasite generates circular zones of attachment could be due to periodic release of adhesins such as TgMIC2 from the micronemes.
claims.source: The regularity with which the parasite generates the circular zones of attachment on its surface, yielding on average one constriction per body length of motion (Figure 5C), could be due to periodic bursts of formin1-mediated actin polymerization at the parasite's apical tip (Tosetti et al., 2019) or to periodic release of adhesins such as TgMIC2 from the micronemes.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the data.

claims.claim: A new constriction may form at the apical tip before the prior constriction has ended, but stalls as the TgMyoA pulls against the adhesive forces of the more posterior previous constriction.
claims.source: Alternatively, the observation that constrictions occur back-to-back almost 50% of the time (Figure 5A), may suggest that a new constriction forms at the apical tip before the prior constriction has ended, but this new constriction stalls as the TgMyoA (or possibly TgMyoH Tosetti et al., 2019) to which it is connected pulls against the adhesive forces of the more posterior previous constriction.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the data with citation to prior work (Tosetti et al., 2019).

claims.claim: The lack of a motility-associated constriction in TgMyoA-deficient parasites could reflect an inability to assemble a ring of adhesins at the apical tip or to move through the incipient ring once it has formed.
claims.source: The lack of a motility-associated constriction in TgMyoA-deficient parasites could reflect an inability either to assemble ring of adhesins at the apical tip of these parasites or, more likely, to move through the incipient ring once it has formed.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the data.

claims.claim: The ring-shaped structures that form during motility may be contractile, and contractility may require TgMyoA.
claims.source: Alternatively, it could be that the ring-shaped structures that form during motility are contractile, and contractility requires TgMyoA.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the data.

claims.claim: The inward deformation of the fibrin matrix towards the constriction is consistent with a contractile ring.
claims.source: The inward deformation of the fibrin matrix towards the constriction reported here is consistent with a contractile ring, as is the physical constriction of the parasite plasma membrane.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental data.

claims.claim: Physical squeezing of the tapering posterior end of the parasite by the narrow constriction may contribute to the parasite's forward motion.
claims.source: This observation suggests that physical squeezing of the tapering posterior end of the parasite by the narrow (and potentially contractile) constriction may contribute to the parasite's forward motion.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the data.

claims.claim: Both wild-type and mutant parasites may generate small forces distributed over their entire surface that are individually below the level of detection.
claims.source: First, it is possible that both the wild-type and mutant parasites generate small forces distributed over their entire surface (in addition to larger forces that may be generated at the constriction in wildtype), which are collectively sufficient to drive motility but individually below our level of detection.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the data.

claims.claim: The loss of TgMyoA or TgMIC2 might lead to compensatory changes in the expression of other genes with overlapping or redundant function.
claims.source: Alternatively, the loss of TgMyoA or TgMIC2 might lead to compensatory changes in the expression of other genes with overlapping or redundant function (Meissner et al., 2013; Frénal and Soldati-Favre, 2015; Lamarque et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is a speculative interpretation with citations to prior work (Meissner et al., 2013; Frénal and Soldati-Favre, 2015; Lamarque et al., 2014).

claims.claim: TgMIC2 knockout parasites show changes in the expression of several other microneme and motility-associated proteins.
claims.source: The TgMIC2 KO parasites do in fact show changes in the expression of several other microneme and motility-associated proteins (Gras et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to published literature (Gras et al., 2017).

claims.claim: Parasites lacking TgMyoA and/or TgMIC2 may use a motility mechanism that is entirely different from that of wild-type parasites.
claims.source: Finally, it is possible that parasites lacking TgMyoA and/or TgMIC2 use a motility mechanism that is entirely different from that of wild-type parasites (e.g., Egarter et al., 2014; Gras et al., 2019) and does not involve a constriction but is nevertheless capable of supporting motility and sustaining the parasite's lytic cycle.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative interpretation with citations to prior work (Egarter et al., 2014; Gras et al., 2019).

claims.claim: Parasites might use different mechanisms for motility in different situations such as squeezing through tight junctions vs. migrating through loose interstitial tissues.
claims.source: By analogy with observations from animal cells (Lämmermann et al., 2008), parasites might use different mechanisms for motility in different situations such as squeezing through tight junctions (Barragan et al., 2005) vs. migrating through loose interstitial tissues.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative interpretation with citations to prior work (Lämmermann et al., 2008; Barragan et al., 2005).

claims.claim: Engagement of T. gondii with the extracellular matrix through a circular band of adhesion may function as part of a guidance system to help the parasite move efficiently through various environments.
claims.source: Engagement of T. gondii with the extracellular matrix through a circular band of adhesion may therefore not only create a fixed platform for the parasite to pull against and move forward; it may also function as part of a guidance system to help the parasite move efficiently through the various environments it encounters as it disseminates through the tissues of the unfortunate organisms it infects.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the data.

claims.claim: A curved cell shape and helical trajectory are a particularly efficient way for small cells to move through viscous media.
claims.source: Extensive studies of the helical swimming behavior of bacteria have shown that a curved cell shape and helical trajectory are a particularly efficient way for small cells to move through viscous media (Berg and Turner, 1979; Ferrero and Lee, 1988; Hazell et al., 1986; Kaiser and Doetsch, 1975; Kimsey and Spielman, 1990).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Berg and Turner, 1979; Ferrero and Lee, 1988; Hazell et al., 1986; Kaiser and Doetsch, 1975; Kimsey and Spielman, 1990).

claims.claim: Annular constrictions that remain stationary relative to the surrounding environment have been reported along the length of Plasmodium ookinetes as they move through peritrophic membrane and microvillar network of the mosquito midgut.
claims.source: Annular constrictions that remain stationary relative to the surrounding environment have also previously been reported along the length of Plasmodium ookinetes as they move through peritrophic membrane and microvillar network of the mosquito midgut (Freyvogel, 1966; Vlachou et al., 2004; Zieler and Dvorak, 2000), suggesting that parasite-generated circular zones of attachment to the environment may be a conserved feature of apicomplexan motility in 3D.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature (Freyvogel, 1966; Vlachou et al., 2004; Zieler and Dvorak, 2000).

claims.claim: Parasite-generated circular zones of attachment to the environment may be a conserved feature of apicomplexan motility in 3D.
claims.source: Annular constrictions that remain stationary relative to the surrounding environment have also previously been reported along the length of Plasmodium ookinetes as they move through peritrophic membrane and microvillar network of the mosquito midgut (Freyvogel, 1966; Vlachou et al., 2004; Zieler and Dvorak, 2000), suggesting that parasite-generated circular zones of attachment to the environment may be a conserved feature of apicomplexan motility in 3D.
claims.evidence: This claim is inferred from observations in multiple apicomplexan species with citation support (Freyvogel, 1966; Vlachou et al., 2004; Zieler and Dvorak, 2000).

results.result: Moving T. gondii parasites exert detectable forces on the surrounding extracellular matrix. Fluorescent microspheres embedded in Matrigel are displaced toward moving parasites from all directions and return to their original positions after the parasite passes.
results.evaluation: Claims C20-C22 are supported by direct experimental observations shown in Figure 1B and Videos 1-2. The bead displacement assay provides clear visual evidence that parasites generate forces on the matrix, with microspheres moving toward the parasite and then relaxing back, demonstrating the elastic nature of the interaction.

results.result: Constrictions form at the apical end of moving parasites and remain stationary relative to the matrix as the parasite moves through. All wild-type parasites that move at least one body length form at least one constriction.
results.evaluation: Claims C23-C25 are well-supported by experimental data from 99 parasites showing 100% constriction formation (C25), with visual documentation in Figure 1C and Video 3 (C23-C24). The sample size is adequate and the observation is consistent across all parasites examined.

results.result: Parasite motility and matrix deformation in fibrin matrices are comparable to those observed in Matrigel.
results.evaluation: Claims C26-C27 are supported by quantitative comparison data in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1, showing no significant differences in motility parameters between fibrin and Matrigel. Visual confirmation of matrix deformation is provided in Figure 2C and Video 5.

results.result: The 3D traction force mapping system has a displacement detection threshold of 42-46 nm in 3D (28-31 nm in x-y plane), corresponding to minimal detectable forces of 0.66-0.72 pN in 3D (0.45-0.49 pN in x-y plane). The fibrin matrix behaves as a predominantly elastic material with an elastic modulus of 15.6 pN/µm and viscous modulus of 0.09 pN*s/µm.
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C34 are supported by rigorous experimental characterization including validation with parasite-free samples (C28), laser trapping measurements (C30-C32), and appropriate calculations converting displacement to force (C33-C34). The methods are well-described and the validation approach is sound.

results.result: The matrix deforms inward toward the parasite from all directions at discrete, periodic time points, then relaxes back to its initial position. This occurs in all three dimensions simultaneously, with deformation either occurring rapidly (50% of cases) or being held through multiple time points before relaxing.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C40 are well-supported by 3D traction force mapping data shown in Figures 4A-D, Videos 6-8, and supplementary figures. The temporal dynamics are quantified (C38-C39) and the 3D nature is demonstrated through multi-axis projections (C37). Background periods show minimal deformation (C40), validating the specificity of the observations.

results.result: Matrix deformation coincides temporally and spatially with parasite constrictions, with displacement vectors pointing inward toward the constriction. This indicates the constriction results from parasite-generated pulling forces rather than the parasite squeezing through pores.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C43 are strongly supported by overlaid force maps and parasite images (Figure 4C-D, Figure 4—figure supplement 3). The directionality of force vectors (inward rather than outward) provides compelling evidence for the pulling mechanism interpretation (C43), though this remains an inference from the data.

results.result: Parasites take 1.6-56.2 seconds (average 6.8±5.2 s) to move through a constriction, with variable timing between successive constrictions. In 46% of cases constrictions occur back-to-back, and in 14% a second constriction begins before the first finishes. Parasite speed increases once the constriction passes the midpoint.
results.evaluation: Claims C44-C47 are supported by quantitative analysis of 99 parasites and 188 constrictions (C44), with detailed temporal analysis shown in Figure 5A-B and Video 9 (C45-C46). The speed analysis (C47) is based on 20 parasites and 24 constrictions shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

results.result: All parasites moving at least one body length undergo constrictions, and trajectory length is directly proportional to the number of constrictions. This suggests constriction-associated forces play an important role in forward movement.
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C50 are supported by data from 99 parasites shown in Figure 5C. The 100% correlation (C48) and linear relationship (C49) provide strong evidence, though the causal interpretation (C50) remains inferential. The proportionality strongly suggests but does not definitively prove the mechanistic role.

results.result: Parasite width decreases from 2.6±0.4 µm to 1.4±0.2 µm at constrictions, forcing the nucleus (normal diameter 2.0±0.3 µm) to deform. The nucleus becomes elongated (width/length ratio changes from 0.93±0.08 to 0.50±0.06) as it passes through constrictions, then regains its round shape.
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C55 are supported by quantitative measurements from 15 parasites/19 constrictions (C51) and 9 parasites/21 constrictions (C55), with visual documentation in Figure 5D-E. The measurements are precise with appropriate error estimates, and the nuclear deformation is clearly demonstrated.

results.result: Fluorescent anti-TgSAG1 antibody is swept from anterior to posterior at constrictions and shed as a helical trail behind moving parasites. All moving parasites examined (n=9) deposited such trails.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C58 are supported by experimental observations in Figure 5—figure supplement 2 and Video 10. The sample size (n=9) is modest but the 100% consistency (C58) and clear visual evidence support the claims. This phenomenon parallels antibody shedding during invasion.

results.result: TgMyoA knockout parasites show severely reduced motility (2% vs 36% moving >1 body length) and altered movement patterns (tightly twisting arcs, stair-like patterns) without forming constrictions. These parasites produce no detectable matrix displacement above background, suggesting forces below the detection limit of 0.66-0.72 pN.
results.evaluation: Claims C59-C65 are supported by analysis of 769 TgMyoA KO parasites compared to 278 WT parasites (C59-C60), with force mapping of 16 KO parasites (C64). The lack of constrictions (C61) and altered trajectories (C62) are documented in Figure 6A and Video 11. The absence of detectable forces (C63-C64) is clearly shown in Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1, though the interpretation that forces are below detection (C65) is inferential.

results.result: TgMIC2 knockout parasites show a less severe motility defect than TgMyoA KO (12% vs 2% moving >1 body length) but move erratically in tightly twisting arcs. These parasites fail to form constrictions and do not detectably deform the matrix, despite moving at speeds similar to wild-type.
results.evaluation: Claims C66-C71 are supported by analysis of 297 TgMIC2 KO parasites (C67), with force mapping of 36 and 18 parasites (C69-C70). The movement patterns are documented in Figure 6A and Video 12 (C68). The claim about similar maximum speeds (C71) relies on citation to Gras et al., 2017. The combination of normal speed but no detectable forces is puzzling and warrants further investigation.

results.result: Both TgMyoA and TgMIC2 are required for constriction formation and constriction-associated inward forces, though motility is significantly altered but not eliminated in their absence.
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C73 are supported by the combined data from both knockout lines showing absence of constrictions and detectable forces in both mutants, while some residual motility persists. This is a reasonable inference from the experimental data, though the mechanistic interpretation requires further validation.

results.result: TgMIC2 knockout parasite nuclei do not change shape during movement. While trajectory lengths are similar to wild-type (38±9 µm vs 42±8 µm), TgMIC2 KO parasites move only half as far from their starting point, suggesting the circumferential attachment zone converts meandering motility into directed progression.
results.evaluation: Claims C74-C77 are supported by nuclear shape analysis (Figure 7A, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A) and trajectory analysis from 1,399 WT and 165 TgMIC2 KO trajectories (Figure 7B, Figure 7—figure supplement 1B). The interpretation that TgMIC2-mediated attachment provides directionality (C77) is a reasonable inference from the reduced displacement-to-length ratio.

results.result: The predominant forces exerted by moving parasites are periodic and directed inward toward a fixed circular location in the matrix, generated by the parasite pulling on the matrix. This ring of inward-directed force corresponds to a circumferential attachment zone through which the parasite propels itself forward.
results.evaluation: Claims C78-C79 are well-supported by the 3D traction force mapping data throughout the manuscript. However, C80 represents a proposed model/interpretation rather than direct experimental evidence. While the model is consistent with all observations, the claim that forces correspond to an attachment zone is speculative and requires additional validation.

results.result: TgMIC2-deficient parasites lack both inward-directed forces and membrane constrictions, and their trajectories are less straight than wild-type. This suggests the annular TgMIC2-mediated attachment zone normally constrains directional options during migration.
results.evaluation: Claims C81-C82 are directly supported by experimental data from TgMIC2 KO parasites. The interpretation about directional constraint (C83) is a reasonable inference from the trajectory analysis, though it remains a proposed mechanism rather than directly demonstrated causation.

results.result: TgMIC2 likely plays an analogous role during motility to TgAMA1 during invasion, binding to matrix ligands rather than TgRON2. 3D motility can be described as sequential invasion-like events through circular attachment zones. The constriction during invasion may reflect pulling on the host membrane rather than being squeezed through.
results.evaluation: Claims C91, C99, and C100 represent interpretive models and speculative hypotheses rather than directly demonstrated results. While these interpretations are consistent with the data and draw interesting parallels between motility and invasion, they lack direct experimental validation. C100 explicitly contradicts prior interpretations and would require additional experiments to confirm.

results.result: The authors propose modifications to the linear motor model where force is generated by actin translocation at the circular attachment ring. They suggest constriction periodicity could result from periodic actin polymerization or adhesin release, or from stalling of new constrictions against previous ones. The constrictions may be contractile and contribute to forward motion through squeezing.
results.evaluation: Claims C103-C111 represent proposed mechanisms and speculative interpretations. While C104 (no anterior-posterior bias detected) is supported by data, the mechanistic proposals (C103, C105-C109, C111) and the interpretation of contractility (C109-C110) lack direct experimental validation. These are reasonable hypotheses that require future testing.

results.result: The authors propose several alternative explanations for residual motility in knockout parasites: forces below detection limits distributed over the surface, compensatory gene expression changes, entirely different motility mechanisms, or context-dependent use of different mechanisms.
results.evaluation: Claims C112, C113, C115, and C116 are explicitly speculative proposals for future investigation. While C114 (TgMIC2 KO shows expression changes) is supported by citation, the other claims represent hypotheses to explain the puzzling observation of motility without detectable forces. These require experimental testing.

results.result: Background on T. gondii: The parasite infects 30-40% of the world's population, causes typically subclinical infections in immunocompetent individuals but can cause blindness or be life-threatening in immunocompromised individuals. The tachyzoite stage uses unique substrate-dependent motility without cilia/flagella, moving up to 3 µm/s along helical trajectories in 3D matrices.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C10 represent well-established background information supported by appropriate citations to the literature. These are not novel findings but provide necessary context for the study.

results.result: Background on the linear motor model: Motility is driven by the glideosome complex, where TgMyoA translocates actin filaments bound to transmembrane adhesins like TgMIC2. The model predicts continuous anterior-to-posterior forces. Similar proteins in other apicomplexans suggest conservation, though recent observations have raised questions about the model.
results.evaluation: Claims C11-C19 represent established background on the linear motor model with appropriate citations. C17 and C18 correctly note both supporting evidence and recent questions about the model, providing balanced context for the current study.

results.result: Parallels between invasion and motility: During invasion, parasites form a moving junction that is anchored to the host cytoskeleton, and the parasite narrows as it passes through. TgAMA1 and TgRON2 are central to junction formation but not motility. Both processes involve rotation around the long axis and may involve helical actin flow. Antibody shedding occurs in both invasion and 3D motility.
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C92 and C97 represent established knowledge with appropriate citations. C90 is supported by citations and unpublished data. C93-C94 cite prior models. C95-C96 are interpretive inferences. C98 is a novel observation supported by Figure 5—figure supplement 2 and Video 10. The parallels drawn are well-supported.

results.result: Background on actin dynamics: Actin polymerization is nucleated at the apical tip by formin1, and anterior-to-posterior actin flux may occur along the entire parasite periphery.
results.evaluation: Claims C101-C102 are supported by appropriate citations to published literature (Tosetti et al., 2019; Hueschen et al., 2022; Quadt et al., 2016; Stadler et al., 2017). These provide necessary background for the discussion.

results.result: The circular attachment zone may function as a guidance system for efficient movement through various environments. Helical trajectories are efficient for small cells in viscous media. Similar annular constrictions have been observed in Plasmodium ookinetes, suggesting this may be a conserved feature of apicomplexan 3D motility.
results.evaluation: Claim C117 is speculative interpretation. C118 is well-supported by multiple citations about bacterial motility. C119-C120 are supported by citations to observations in Plasmodium, making a reasonable inference about conservation. The speculation about guidance (C117) is reasonable but untested.
